explain.say: Chlorine keeps swimming pools clean, and iodine cleans cuts. They are cousins in group 7, called the halogens. But one is far fiercer than the other. Look at the board, and you will find out why.

faq.q: Why does reactivity decrease down group 7?
faq.a: Going down, halogen atoms get bigger, so the outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded. The pull on an incoming electron is weaker, so they react less easily.
asks: Why is fluorine the most reactive halogen?

faq.q: What is a halogen displacement reaction?
faq.a: A more reactive halogen takes the place of a less reactive one in a salt. Chlorine plus potassium bromide gives potassium chloride plus bromine.
At room temperature, fluorine is a pale yellow gas, chlorine a green-yellow gas, bromine a red-brown liquid, and iodine a grey-black solid that gives a purple vapour.

faq.q: Why are halogens used to kill germs?
faq.a: Chlorine and iodine are reactive enough to damage the cells of bacteria. Small amounts of chlorine keep tap water and pools safe.
asks: Why is chlorine put in pools?

faq.q: Why do halogens form negative ions?
faq.a: A halogen atom has 7 outer electrons and gains one more to fill its shell. With one extra electron it becomes a negative ion with a charge of minus 1, like chloride.

facts: Halogens become less reactive down group 7; fluorine is the most reactive.
Bromine is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature; the other is mercury.
